note: No authentic anchor in the sample corpus. Rely on the rubric card at docs/taxonomy/LR/role_in_argument.md and use LSAT prose conventions from neighboring samples for voice calibration only.

samples.reason: Voice calibration only — method-of-reasoning item. Role-in-argument items share the descriptor-style credited-answer voice but ask about a SPECIFIC claim's function rather than the overall argument's method.

question.difficultyReason: Abstract answer descriptions require matching a concrete scenario to a highly-general logical operation. Two traps (A) and (E) use causal/predictive language that sounds plausible but does not describe what the executive actually did.
question.stimulus: Executive: We recently ran a set of advertisements in the print version of a travel magazine and on that magazine's website. We were unable to get any direct information about consumer response to the print ads. However, we found that consumer response to the ads on the website was much more limited than is typical for website ads. We concluded that consumer response to the print ads was probably below par as well.
question.questionStem: The executive's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: bases a prediction of the intensity of a phenomenon on information about the intensity of that phenomenon's cause

choices.label: B
choices.text: uses information about the typical frequency of events of a general kind to draw a conclusion about the probability of a particular event of that kind

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a statistical generalization from claims about a large number of specific instances

choices.label: D
choices.text: uses a case in which direct evidence is available to draw a conclusion about an analogous case in which direct evidence is unavailable

choices.label: E
choices.text: bases a prediction about future events on facts about recent comparable events

explanations.correct: The executive has direct data about the website ads, no direct data about the print ads, and uses the analogy between the two campaigns to infer the print performance. That is exactly what D describes.
explanations.A: The argument is about analogous response, not cause-and-intensity.
explanations.B: No 'typical frequency of events of a general kind' is invoked.
explanations.C: There is only one analogous instance, not a large number.
explanations.E: The conclusion is about the same campaign as the evidence, not about future events.

source.notes: Verbatim from LSAC public LR sample page. Correct answer D confirmed.

samples.reason: Voice calibration only — principle-justify item. Provides a model of the dense, multi-claim stimulus structure role-in-argument questions typically inhabit.

question.difficultyReason: Requires selecting the principle that most directly licenses the specific claim about middle-class members of poor nations. Trap (D) makes a sweeping claim that superficially matches.
question.stimulus: Journalist: To reconcile the need for profits sufficient to support new drug research with the moral imperative to provide medicines to those who most need them but cannot afford them, some pharmaceutical companies feel justified in selling a drug in rich nations at one price and in poor nations at a much lower price. But this practice is unjustified. A nation with a low average income may still have a substantial middle class better able to pay for new drugs than are many of the poorer citizens of an overall wealthier nation.
question.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the journalist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: People who are ill deserve more consideration than do healthy people, regardless of their relative socioeconomic positions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Wealthy institutions have an obligation to expend at least some of their resources to assist those incapable of assisting themselves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether one deserves special consideration depends on one's needs rather than on characteristics of the society to which one belongs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The people in wealthy nations should not have better access to health care than do the people in poorer nations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unequal access to health care is more unfair than an unequal distribution of wealth.

explanations.correct: The journalist's complaint is that pricing by nation ignores the fact that individual ability-to-pay varies within and across nations. Principle C — deserving consideration depends on individual needs, not society-level characteristics — directly underwrites that critique.
explanations.A: Concerns illness vs. health, not rich-nation vs. poor-nation.
explanations.B: Institutional obligation is not the journalist's subject.
explanations.D: Inverts the journalist's point — the journalist isn't arguing for equal access but against nation-level pricing.
explanations.E: Comparative fairness is not what the journalist is defending.

source.notes: Verbatim from LSAC public LR sample page. Correct answer C confirmed.
